If you're wondering...

Why do some plants work so well together?

Companion planting is often presented as a list of "good neighbors" and "bad neighbors," as if plants simply like each other or not. That story is easy to remember, but it hides what's actually going on. Behind every good combination is a concrete mechanism — something one plant does, gives, or needs, that happens to line up exactly with what the other plant needs or specifically doesn't need. Once you know that mechanism, you can come up with new combinations yourself instead of having to follow a list.

The best-known example is the classic trio of corn, beans, and squash. Corn grows tall and provides a sturdy stalk; beans climb up it instead of needing a stake of their own, and meanwhile fix nitrogen from the air into the soil — nitrogen that corn, a real heavy feeder, happens to need a lot of. Squash crawls along the ground below, shading the soil against drying out and weeds, and keeps unwanted visitors at bay with its bristly leaves. Three plants, three different functions, that complement each other exactly without getting in each other's way.

That pattern — complementing rather than competing — shows up again and again, even in less well-known pairings. A plant with a deep taproot draws water and minerals from further down than a plant with shallow, branching roots, so the two don't have to fight over the same layer in the same soil. Strongly scented herbs like basil or marigolds mask the scent pest insects use to find their host plant, quietly protecting the vegetable next to them. Some plants attract predatory insects that clean up their neighbor's pests. And just as surely, real bad combinations exist too: plants that share the same diseases, or that release substances that actually inhibit a neighbor's growth instead of supporting it — allelopathy, the chemical mirror image of cooperation.

What companion planting ultimately is, is nothing more than the principle of diversity applied at the smallest scale: not a hundred species mixed together, but two or three species you deliberately place side by side because you know what each one gives and needs. Following a list works, but understanding why it works lets you combine plants yourself, based on what you actually see happening in your own garden.

Good neighbors don't exist by accident. They exist because one gives what the other needs, or removes what threatens the other.
